turns.prompt: I'd like to understand the history of tea in Britain. How did it become so popular?
turns.response:
Tea became popular in Britain through a combination of **fashion, falling prices, imperial trade and everyday social habits**. It began as something expensive to show off; eventually it became something ordinary to offer a guest. That transformation took roughly two centuries. ([rct.uk](https://www.rct.uk/collection/stories/tea-in-the-royal-collection))

### 1. A fashionable foreign luxury: the 1650s–1700s
Tea arrived from China and appeared in London coffeehouses in the 1650s. Catherine of Braganza, the Portuguese princess who married Charles II in **1662**, helped make it fashionable at court. She didn’t introduce tea to Britain, but her example gave it aristocratic prestige. The East India Company then helped supply the growing demand. ([rct.uk](https://www.rct.uk/collection/stories/tea-in-the-royal-collection))

It was expensive enough that wealthy households kept it in **locked tea caddies**. Serving tea, with fine porcelain and elaborate equipment, was a way to display both money and manners. ([nationaltrust.org.uk](https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/discover/history/the-history-of-tea))

### 2. Sugar and sociability widened its appeal
During the eighteenth century, increasing imports brought tea within reach of more households. Drinking it became a domestic social ritual, as well as something people enjoyed in pleasure gardens and spa towns. Sugar helped make it appealing—but that sweetness depended heavily on Caribbean plantations worked by enslaved Africans. Tea’s familiar domestic history and Britain’s colonial history are inseparable. ([londonmuseum.org.uk](https://www.londonmuseum.org.uk/blog/steeped-in-history-tea-drinking-in-britain/))

### 3. Smugglers—and then a tax cut—made it more affordable
High taxes kept legal tea costly, so smugglers supplied a substantial market. Importantly, ordinary people were already developing a taste for tea before the government made it cheaper.

The major turning point came in **1784**, when the Commutation Act reduced tea taxes from **119% to 12.5%**. That severely undercut smuggling and made legally imported tea much more accessible. So tea wasn’t simply a fashion that trickled down: its spread also depended on a dramatic change in price. ([rmg.co.uk](https://www.rmg.co.uk/stories/maritime-history/cutty-sark-tea-trade))

### 4. Nineteenth-century empire expanded the supply
Britain initially depended heavily on Chinese tea. British commercial efforts to offset the cost included trafficking Indian-grown opium into China—a trade entangled with the Opium Wars. Later, expanding production in British-controlled India and Ceylon, now Sri Lanka, brought cheaper supplies onto the British market. ([rmg.co.uk](https://www.rmg.co.uk/stories/maritime-history/cutty-sark-tea-trade))

These plantations didn’t *start* Britain’s enthusiasm for tea: they supplied and expanded an already substantial appetite. By the 1820s, Britain was already being described as a tea-drinking nation. ([londonmuseum.org.uk](https://www.londonmuseum.org.uk/blog/steeped-in-history-tea-drinking-in-britain/))

### 5. It acquired a place in the daily routine
Tea became embedded in meals, hospitality and work breaks. Some employers supplied it to workers; temperance campaigners promoted it as an alternative to alcohol. Meanwhile, fashionable **afternoon tea**, with sandwiches and cakes, developed in the 1840s—much later than tea-drinking itself. Working-class **high tea** was something different: a substantial meal accompanied by tea, not a grander version of afternoon tea. ([rmg.co.uk](https://www.rmg.co.uk/stories/maritime-history/cutty-sark-tea-trade))

The useful distinction is this: **prestige helped people want tea; cheaper supply let them buy it; daily rituals made the habit stick.** The famously British cup was the result of a thoroughly international—and often exploitative—history. ([londonmuseum.org.uk](https://www.londonmuseum.org.uk/blog/steeped-in-history-tea-drinking-in-britain/))

turns.prompt: What was the role of the East India Company in all that?
turns.response:
The East India Company was **the main commercial link between Britain’s growing appetite for tea and its Asian suppliers**. But it wasn’t simply a shipping business: it became a colonial power with its own armies and territories. That combination made its role unusually consequential. ([nationaltrust.org.uk](https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/discover/history/what-was-the-east-india-company?utm_source=openai))

**1. It controlled the legal supply.**  
The Company held a monopoly on importing tea into Britain from China. Its trade helped supply the expanding market—but monopoly did not mean cheap tea, or control of every cup. Smuggling was enormous: in the early 1780s, estimated British consumption was more than twice the Company’s recorded tea sales. ([nationaltrust.org.uk](https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/discover/history/what-was-the-east-india-company?utm_source=openai))

**2. It connected tea drinking to the opium trade.**  
Buying Chinese tea required large amounts of silver. To help finance that trade, the Company used its control over production in India to supply opium for the illegal Chinese market. Tea, silver and opium became parts of the same commercial system: Britain’s domestic habit was tied to exploitation far beyond Britain. ([lib.cam.ac.uk](https://www.lib.cam.ac.uk/rcs/projects-exhibitions/opium-morally-indefensible-trade-horrible-drug/opium-captions?utm_source=openai))

**3. It helped develop an alternative to Chinese tea.**  
Under Company rule, a Tea Committee was established in India in **1834** to investigate production in Assam. Company officials promoted plantations, allocated land to Europeans and supported a system dependent on poorly paid Indian labour. This helped lay the foundations for Britain’s later reliance on Indian-grown tea. ([globalcapitalism.history.ox.ac.uk](https://globalcapitalism.history.ox.ac.uk/files/case33-englisheastindiacompanypdf?utm_source=openai))

**4. Its monopoly ended before the tea industry’s later expansion.**  
Parliament abolished its remaining China-tea monopoly in **1833**, opening the way for other traders. So it’s important not to credit the Company with the entire subsequent story of British tea. ([parliament.uk](https://www.parliament.uk/about/living-heritage/evolutionofparliament/legislativescrutiny/parliament-and-empire/parliament-and-the-american-colonies-before-1765/east-india-company-and-raj-1785-1858/?utm_source=openai))

In short: **it supplied the habit, profited from controlling that supply, and helped reshape Asian production and trade to sustain it.** It was both a tea merchant and an imperial power—not two separate careers, but closely connected ones. ([nationaltrust.org.uk](https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/discover/history/what-was-the-east-india-company?utm_source=openai))

turns.prompt: And when did tea bags appear, and why did they catch on?
turns.response:
**Tea bags emerged around the turn of the twentieth century—but Britain took another half-century to begin adopting them seriously.** Their great selling point was less mess, rather than better tea. ([guinnessworldrecords.com](https://www.guinnessworldrecords.com/world-records/630511-first-teabags))

### When did they appear?
There wasn’t one clean moment of invention. Roberta Lawson and Mary McLaren patented a mesh **“Tea Leaf Holder” in 1903**, and even that had earlier predecessors. ([guinnessworldrecords.com](https://www.guinnessworldrecords.com/world-records/630511-first-teabags))

The famous story concerns New York tea merchant **Thomas Sullivan, around 1908**: he sent samples in silk pouches, and customers supposedly brewed the tea inside them rather than emptying them out. It’s an appealing origin story, but not reliable evidence that he invented the tea bag. Later developments in inexpensive porous paper helped make bags practical for mass production. ([guinnessworldrecords.com](https://www.guinnessworldrecords.com/world-records/630511-first-teabags))

### When did Britain take to them?
**Tetley’s 1953 launch was an important commercial push**, not an overnight conversion. Tea bags still accounted for **less than 3% of the British market in the early 1960s**; by 2007, their share had reached **96%**, according to the UK Tea & Infusions Association. ([tetley.com](https://www.tetley.com/history-tetley))

### Why did they catch on?
They removed several small nuisances at once: no strainer, no loose leaves to empty from the pot, and an easy way to brew directly in a mug. That fitted the postwar enthusiasm for labour-saving household products. The industry association specifically identifies **easier cleanup** as a major reason for British adoption. ([tea.co.uk](https://www.tea.co.uk/the-history-of-the-tea-bag))

So this was a different transformation from the one we’ve been discussing: **tea had already become an everyday drink; the bag made preparing it an easier everyday task.** ([tea.co.uk](https://www.tea.co.uk/the-history-of-the-tea-bag))
